explanations.answer: Keeps him and won't let him go home
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Saul, king of Israel, kept David with him from that day, and the text says he did not let David return to his father's house. David had been going back and forth between the palace and his dad's sheep (1 Samuel 17:15). Now the commute is over.

explanations.answer: Sends him back to his father's sheep
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think that, since David used to go back and forth to the sheep (1 Samuel 17:15). But after Goliath, the text says Saul kept David with him. He did not let David return to his father's house. The sheep will have to manage without him for now.

explanations.answer: Sends him home with great riches
explanations.explanation: Nice thought, but no treasure wagon rolls out of the palace here. The text says Saul kept David with him and did not let him return to his father's house. David isn't going home at all. Saul wants him close.

Yes! Jonathan, Saul's son, gave David his robe, then his tunic, his sword, his bow and his belt. That's a prince handing over his own gear. I once gave a neighbor a spare oven mitt and felt generous, so this is a whole other level.

Close to the spirit of it, but not what the text lists. Verse 4 says Jonathan gave David his robe, his tunic, his sword, his bow and his belt. No horse and no servants are mentioned. Still, he gave the clothes right off his back, so the gift was no small thing.

That would be a big move, but the text doesn't say it. Jonathan removed his robe and gave it to David, along with his tunic, his sword, his bow and his belt. Everything on the list is something he carried or wore. No deed to a house in sight.

Right. The text says David's rise was pleasing in the sight of all the people, and of Saul's officers as well. Everybody was on board, officers included. Hold onto that, because one person's feelings are about to change.

Here's what the text actually says. After Saul set David over the men of war, it was pleasing in the sight of all the people, and of Saul's officers as well. So the people and the officers were both pleased. It's a good moment, and it doesn't stay quiet for long.
Not quite, friend. Listen to the lyrics: “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.” Thousands for Saul, tens of thousands for David. David gets the bigger number.

Right. The women sang, “Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.” Saul gets thousands, but David gets tens of thousands. It's a catchy tune, and I think one of its listeners is not clapping along.

explanations.answer: He is furious and resents it
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says Saul was furious and resented the song. He said, “They have ascribed tens of thousands to David, but only thousands to me.” One little number difference, and he can't let it go.

explanations.answer: He joins right in and sings
explanations.explanation: Picture it, though. Saul in the middle of the parade, belting out a song where the other guy gets the bigger number. The text says the opposite: Saul was furious and resented the song. No sing-along from him.

explanations.answer: He is proud of David for it
explanations.explanation: That would've been a sweet ending, but it isn't what the text says. Saul was furious and resented the song. Then he asked, “What more can he have but the kingdom?” That's not a proud dad moment.
That's the word. From that day forward, Saul kept a jealous eye on David. The song ended, but the stare didn't. Once he started watching David that way, there was no stopping.
You'd hope so, since David had just taken down Goliath (1 Samuel 17:50). But the verse doesn't say that. It says Saul kept a jealous eye on David from that day forward. Not grateful, jealous.
That's a warm word, but it doesn't fit the verse. After the song, the text says Saul kept a jealous eye on David. A fatherly eye would be a lot more relaxed. This one watches closely.

Yes. Saul hurled the spear, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” I think this is a heavy moment, because David had just been playing the harp in that room. David was playing, and Saul was aiming.

I wish it had gone that way. But the text says Saul hurled the spear, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” I think this part is heavy, so I'm not going to joke about it. Nobody was handed anything.

explanations.answer: He sets it down to listen
explanations.explanation: A peaceful harp concert would've been nice. But the text says Saul hurled the spear, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story. The spear didn't get set down.
Not this time, friend. Saul hurled the spear, but the text says David eluded him twice. No pinning happened. David got away from it both times.
Right. Saul hurled the spear, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” But David eluded him twice. The plan didn't work, and David walked away.

explanations.answer: The LORD was with David and had left Saul
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says Saul was afraid of David because the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul. That's the reason the verse gives. It's not about who has the bigger army, it's about who the LORD is with.

explanations.answer: Samuel had warned Saul about David
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess, but this passage never says it. The reason in verse 12 is that the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul. Nobody's warning is mentioned. We stick with what the text gives.

explanations.answer: David had threatened to take the throne
explanations.explanation: That's a guess the text never makes. Verse 12 says Saul was afraid because the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul. David's name and the word threat don't show up together in this verse. Saul's own words about the kingdom were in verse 8, but they weren't a threat from David.

Yes. David continued to prosper in all his ways, because the LORD was with him. Send him out with a thousand men, and he still thrives. Meanwhile I once sent a batch out of the oven too early and it came back flat.

No wandering for this guy. The text says he led the troops out to battle and back, and he continued to prosper in all his ways. The reason given is that the LORD was with him. He knew where he was going.
You'd think a new command might be rough, but the text says otherwise. David continued to prosper in all his ways, because the LORD was with him. Struggling isn't in the verse. Prospering is.

explanations.answer: He leads them out to battle and back
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. The text says all Israel and Judah loved David because he was leading them out to battle and back. They saw him lead and come home. Saul sent him away, and the whole country still loved him.

explanations.answer: He shares Goliath's plunder with them
explanations.explanation: I get the idea, but the text doesn't say that. Verse 16 says they loved David because he was leading them out to battle and back. No plunder is handed around in this verse. It's his leading that wins them.

explanations.answer: He promises them a new king soon
explanations.explanation: That's not in this verse. The text says Israel and Judah loved David because he was leading them out to battle and back. David doesn't promise anyone anything here. They love what they see him do.

explanations.answer: Let the Philistines strike David down
explanations.explanation: Yes. Saul said to David, “Only be valiant for me and fight the LORD’s battles.” But Saul was thinking, “I need not raise my hand against him; let the hand of the Philistines be against him.” The Philistines are Israel's enemies in these battles. The offer sounds kind, but Saul's thoughts tell a different story.

explanations.answer: David will make a fine son-in-law
explanations.explanation: That's what the offer sounds like out loud. But the text shows what Saul was really thinking: “I need not raise my hand against him; let the hand of the Philistines be against him.” So it wasn't about a fine son-in-law. Saul's words and thoughts don't match.

explanations.answer: Merab will keep David loyal to him
explanations.explanation: That makes sense on paper, but the text doesn't say it. Saul's thought was, “I need not raise my hand against him; let the hand of the Philistines be against him.” Loyalty isn't mentioned. His thoughts are about the Philistines.

explanations.answer: He asks who he is to become the king's son-in-law
explanations.explanation: Yes. David said, “Who am I, and what is my family or my father’s clan in Israel, that I should become the son-in-law of the king?” He doesn't jump at the chance. I think he's being humble, and he's not asking for a thing.

explanations.answer: He asks for land and riches to go along with her
explanations.explanation: That's not what David says. He asks, “Who am I, and what is my family or my father’s clan in Israel, that I should become the son-in-law of the king?” There's no list of demands. He's asking about himself, not about the deal.

explanations.answer: He asks to fight the Philistines before the wedding
explanations.explanation: The Philistines come up later, but David doesn't ask for that here. His answer is, “Who am I, and what is my family or my father’s clan in Israel, that I should become the son-in-law of the king?” He's wondering if he's even the right guy. The battle talk comes after.
Not quite. The text says that when it was time to give Merab to David, she was given in marriage to Adriel of Meholah. So David never got her. The offer fell through.
Right. When it was time, Saul's daughter Merab was given in marriage to Adriel of Meholah. She never went to David. The promise didn't stick.

explanations.answer: She can be a snare to David
explanations.explanation: Yes. Saul thought, “I will give her to David, so that she may be a snare to him, and the hand of the Philistines may be against him.” Michal loves David, and Saul uses that for his own plan. I think that's a cold way to treat his own daughter's love.

explanations.answer: She deserves to marry for love
explanations.explanation: It's a sweet thought, but it's not Saul's. The text says he thought, “I will give her to David, so that she may be a snare to him…” That's his plan, and it's about David's trouble. Michal's love just happens to be useful to him.

explanations.answer: She can bring peace to his house
explanations.explanation: I wish the text said that. But Saul's thought was, “I will give her to David, so that she may be a snare to him, and the hand of the Philistines may be against him.” Peace isn't the goal. Saul is still working against David.

That's right. Saul ordered his servants, “Speak to David privately and tell him, ‘Behold, the king is pleased with you, and all his servants love you. Now therefore, become his son-in-law.’” The message comes through the servants, quietly. It's a sneaky setup.

Here's what the text says. Saul ordered his servants, “Speak to David privately and tell him, ‘Behold, the king is pleased with you, and all his servants love you.’” So he did give that order. It's a private message through his servants.

explanations.answer: He is a poor man and not well regarded
explanations.explanation: Yes. David replied, “Does it seem trivial in your sight to be the son-in-law of the king? I am a poor man and lightly esteemed.” He doesn't puff himself up. I honestly respect that, since I'm a stamper who once got all dusty in a drawer.

explanations.answer: He is too busy with the king's battles
explanations.explanation: That's not what he says. David replied, “I am a poor man and lightly esteemed.” He talks about himself, not his schedule. The battles aren't his excuse.

explanations.answer: He is not ready to leave his father's house
explanations.explanation: That's a different story from the one in the verse. David says, “I am a poor man and lightly esteemed.” He's thinking about who he is, not where he lives. Saul had already kept him from going home anyway (1 Samuel 18:2).

Yes. When the servants reported the terms, David was pleased to become the king's son-in-law. Saul's plan was for the Philistines to deal with David. David just saw a chance to be the king's son-in-law.
Here's what the text says. When the servants reported these terms to David, he was pleased to become the king's son-in-law. So he said yes to it. David didn't hesitate or walk away.

Yes, two hundred. David and his men killed two hundred Philistines before the wedding day arrived. Saul asked for a hundred. David doubled it, like a guy who gets asked for one favor and shows up with a truck.
One hundred was Saul's number. David came back with more than that. The text says David and his men killed two hundred Philistines. He doubled the ask.
That's more than the text says. Saul asked for a hundred, and David and his men killed two hundred. Two hundred is already double. We don't need to inflate it.

That's the word. When Saul realized the LORD was with David and that Michal loved David, he grew even more afraid of David. The fear was already there (1 Samuel 18:12), and it grew. The harder Saul tried, the more he saw it.
That would be a nice turn, but the text says something else. Saul grew even more afraid of David. Fond doesn't show up in the verse. Fear was growing.
You'd think a king might be proud of a son-in-law like that. But the text says Saul grew even more afraid of David. Pride isn't in the verse. Fear is.
Not at all, friend. The text says that from then on, Saul was David's enemy. No peace treaty was signed. David had even become his son-in-law, and Saul still saw him that way.
Right. The text says, “So from then on Saul was David’s enemy.” Even after the wedding, nothing got friendlier from Saul's side. It's a hard turn for this story.

Yes. Every time the Philistine commanders came out for battle, David was more successful than all of Saul's officers, so his name was highly esteemed. Remember, David called himself lightly esteemed back in verse 23. Now people say his name with respect.
I can see why you'd wonder, with Saul glaring at him. But the text says David's name was highly esteemed. That means respected, not criticized. The Philistines kept coming, and David kept winning.

I know a little about being forgotten, and this isn't it. The text says David was more successful than all of Saul's officers, so his name was highly esteemed. Everybody knew his name. Forgotten isn't the word.
